# Ensure all tables render inline at 10pt body font size without horizontal overflow or float page isolation,
# and replace em/en-dashes with plain hyphens (-).
sanitize_latex_text <- function (arg0_text, arg1_in_table = FALSE) {
  text <- as.character(arg0_text)
  if (length(text) == 0 || is.na(text) || !nzchar(text)) return("")
  text <- gsub("`", "", text, fixed = TRUE)
  parts <- strsplit(text, "(?<=\\$)|(?=\\$)", perl = TRUE)[[1]]
  in_math <- FALSE
  out_parts <- character(length(parts))
  for (i in seq_along(parts)) {
    p <- parts[i]
    if (identical(p, "$")) {
      in_math <- !in_math
      out_parts[i] <- "$"
    } else if (in_math) {
      p <- gsub("\u2192", " \\rightarrow ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u00d7", " \\times ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u0394", "\\Delta ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u00b2", "^2", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2013", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2014", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("---", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("--", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("(?<!\\\\)%", "\\\\%", p, perl = TRUE)
      out_parts[i] <- p
    } else {
      p <- gsub("\u2192", " to ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u00d7", "x", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u0394", "$\\Delta$", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("km\u00b2", "km\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("m\u00b2", "m\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("R\u00b2", "R\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u00b2", "\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2013", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2014", " - ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("---", " - ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("--", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("(?<!\\\\)&", "\\\\&", p, perl = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("(?<!\\\\)%", "\\\\%", p, perl = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("(?<!\\\\)_", "\\\\_", p, perl = TRUE)
      if (isTRUE(arg1_in_table)) {
        p <- gsub("\\_", "\\_\\allowbreak{}", p, fixed = TRUE)
        p <- gsub("/", "/\\allowbreak{}", p, fixed = TRUE)
        # Keep thousands-separated numbers and BC/AD dates on a single line inside table cells
        p <- gsub("(?<=\\b[1-9][0-9]{0,2}) (?=[0-9]{3}\\b)", ".", p, perl = TRUE)
        p <- gsub("(?<=\\.[0-9]{3}) (?=[0-9]{3}\\b)", ".", p, perl = TRUE)
        p <- gsub("(?<=\\b[1-9][0-9]{0,2}) (?=[0-9]{3}\\b)", ".", p, perl = TRUE)
        p <- gsub("(?<=\\.[0-9]{3}) (?=[0-9]{3}\\b)", ".", p, perl = TRUE)
        p <- gsub("([0-9])\\s*(BC|AD)\\b", "\\1\\2", p, perl = TRUE)
        # Prevent line breaks immediately after a leading negative sign (e.g. -10000)
        p <- gsub("(^|\\s|\\()-([0-9])", "\\1\\\\mbox{-}\\2", p, perl = TRUE)
      }
      out_parts[i] <- p
    }
  }
  return(paste(out_parts, collapse = ""))
}

sanitize_prose_unicode_for_latex <- function (arg0_line) {
  line_str <- as.character(arg0_line)
  if (length(line_str) == 0 || is.na(line_str) || !nzchar(line_str)) return(line_str)
  parts <- strsplit(line_str, "(?<=\\$)|(?=\\$)", perl = TRUE)[[1]]
  in_math <- FALSE
  for (i in seq_along(parts)) {
    p <- parts[i]
    if (identical(p, "$")) {
      in_math <- !in_math
    } else if (in_math) {
      p <- gsub("\u2192", " \\rightarrow ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u00d7", " \\times ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u0394", "\\Delta ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2248", " \\approx ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2013", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2014", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      parts[i] <- p
    } else {
      p <- gsub(
        "\\b(Figures?|Figs?\\.|Tables?|Tabs?\\.|Images?|Definitions?|Sections?|Appendix)(?:\\s+|~)\\\\ref\\{([^}]+)\\}",
        "\\\\crdxref{\\1}{\\2}",
        p,
        perl = TRUE
      )
      p <- gsub("\u2192", " to ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u00d7", "x", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u0394", "$\\Delta$", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2248", "~", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("km\u00b2", "km\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("m\u00b2", "m\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("R\u00b2", "R\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u00b2", "\\textsuperscript{2}", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2013", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("\u2014", " - ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("---", " - ", p, fixed = TRUE)
      p <- gsub("--", "-", p, fixed = TRUE)
      parts[i] <- p
    }
  }
  return(paste(parts, collapse = ""))
}

orig_render_figure_template <- render_figure_template
render_figure_template <- function (arg0_file_path, arg1_options = NULL) {
  options <- if (!is.null(arg1_options)) arg1_options else list()
  options$placement <- "!htbp"
  if (is.null(options$max_height) || identical(options$max_height, "none")) {
    options$max_height <- "0.42\\textheight"
  }
  return(orig_render_figure_template(arg0_file_path, options))
}

# Abstract

Dagestan covers 50,3k km² on the north-eastern flank of the Greater Caucasus between the Caspian Sea and the high mountain crest. Its population history centres on two main areas: the narrow coastal corridor around Derbent and the terraced limestone plateaus of the interior. Farming and herding began early in the mountains at Chokh around 6000BC, supporting roughly 4,5k people [@amirkhanov1987chokh; @amirkhanov2022chokh; @davudov2009]. During the Eneolithic and Early Bronze Age, Kura-Araxes stone villages in the highlands (Ginchi and Chinna) and large coastal mounds at Velikent raised the population to 45k by 3000BC [@gadzhiev1991early; @gadzhiev1997velikent; @magomedov2000kura; @magomedov2005]. In the Middle and Late Bronze Ages, farmers terraced nearly half the land surface of mid-mountain Dagestan (100k-150k ha of stepped fields), allowing numbers to reach 95k by 1000BC [@borisov2013terraces; @korobov2020terraces; @shaev2024terraces; @aglarov1986terraces]. Along the Caspian coast, Sassanian, Khazar and early Islamic walled towns at Derbent, Urtseki, Tarki, Balanjar and Endirey grew alongside the highland clan and village unions (*jamaats*) [@abakarov1993atlas; @kudryavtsev1982derbent; @gadjiev2017derbent; @gmyrya1995huns]. Population reached a medieval peak of 310k (270k-350k) around 1200AD before the Mongol and Timurid invasions reduced it by a quarter to 230k in 1400AD [@ikhilov1960narody; @aliev2017tabasaran; @gasanov2024]. Recovery across the lowland principalities and highland free societies carried numbers to 460k (420k-500k) by 1700AD [@aliev1975feudal; @umakhanov1973mutual; @aglarov1988jamaat]. Despite heavy losses during Nadir Shah's campaigns of 1741-1743 (445k in 1750AD) and the Caucasian War of 1829-1859 (485k in 1850AD), peace after 1860 and the arrival of the railway lifted the population within modern Dagestan to 690k (650k-730k) by 1900AD [@kabuzan1996; @kozubsky1901; @troynitskiy1905dagestan; @nagieva2005].

# Background

Lying between the Caspian Sea (-28 m) and Mount Bazardüzü (4.466 m), Dagestan (50,3k km²) divides into lowlands along the coast and river deltas, and steep plateaus and gorges in the interior.

Along the coast runs the Maritime Caspian Corridor (the Derbent Gate), a narrow plain 3-35 km wide between the eastern spurs of the Caucasus and the sea (Zone 1, 6,8k km²), which opens northward into the semi-arid Terek-Sulak and Kumyk steppes (Zone 4, 13,5k km²). As the main land route between the Eurasian steppe and Iran, this lowland belt held Early Bronze Age mound settlements at Velikent and Kabaz-Kutan, Sassanian border walls and garrisons at Derbent (*Bab al-Abwab*) and Palasa-Syrt, early Khazar towns at Balanjar (Verkhniy Chir-Yurt), Samandar (Tarki), Varachan (Urtseki) and Endirey (Andreyaulem), and the early modern Kumyk and Kaitag principalities [@gadzhiev1997velikent; @kudryavtsev1982derbent; @gadjiev2008palasa; @magomedov1983khazar; @fedchenko2023].

Inland rise the foothills, the Inner Limestone Plateaus and the high Samur gorges (Zones 2 and 3, 30k km²). Cut by the four branches of the Koysu (Andi, Avar, Kara and Kazikumukh, which join to form the Sulak) and by the Samur river, interior Dagestan was one of the earliest centres of mountain grain farming at Chokh (6000BC) and hillside terracing (2000-1000BC) [@amirkhanov1987chokh; @borisov2013terraces; @idrisov2018]. Protected by narrow limestone gorges around Gunib, Khunzakh, Kumukh, Akusha and Kubachi, the mountain villages survived the Mongol and Timurid invasions that repeatedly emptied the coastal plain [@abakarov1993atlas; @aglarov1988jamaat].

# Methodology

## Regional Subdivisions

Following the archaeological survey of Abakarov and Davudov (which mapped 2,1k sites across 38 districts) [@abakarov1993atlas; @budaychiev2014] and the geographical divisions of Gadzhiev [@gadzhiev1991early], we divide Dagestan (50,3k km²) into four elevation zones (Table 1).

## Estimation Methods

Our population estimates rely on five main sources of evidence across successive periods.

For Neolithic and Eneolithic stone villages (Chokh, Ginchi, Chinna and Mekegi) and Early Bronze Age mounds (Velikent) between 6000 and 1000BC, household numbers are estimated from excavated round and rectangular stone houses (12-38 m² floor area, or one family of 4,5-5,5 persons per hearth) and checked against skeleton counts in collective catacomb tombs, which held 100-350 burials per vault over 150-250 years [@gadzhiev1997velikent; @mednikova2020velikent; @kohl2007making; @davudov2014].

For the mountain terrace farming period (1500BC-1200AD), satellite mapping and soil dating show that 48,3% of mid-mountain Dagestan (100k-150k ha) was terraced [@borisov2013terraces; @korobov2020terraces; @shaev2024terraces; @idrisov2018]. The population that these terraces could feed, $K_{\text{terrace}}(t)$, is given by:
   $$K_{\text{terrace}}(t) = \frac{A_{\text{terrace}}(t) \cdot \theta_{\text{active}}(t) \cdot Y_{\text{grain}}}{C_{\text{cap}}}$$
where $A_{\text{terrace}}(t)$ is the total terraced area, $\theta_{\text{active}}(t) \in [0{,}45,\,0{,}65]$ is the share under crops in any given year, $Y_{\text{grain}} \approx 850\text{-}1{,}1\text{k kg/ha}$ is the yield of manured mountain barley and wheat [@aglarov1986terraces] and $C_{\text{cap}} \approx 250\text{ kg/person/yr}$ is annual grain consumption, supplemented by sheep herding.

For the Sassanian, Khazar and early Islamic walled towns (Derbent, Urtseki, Tarki, Balanjar and Endirey) between 400BC and 1220AD, urban populations are estimated from walled area: 100-140 persons/ha in the 30-35 ha residential quarter (*shahristan*) of Derbent, 40-60 persons/ha in the craft suburbs and 10-20 persons/ha in the garrison forts [@kudryavtsev1982derbent; @gadjiev2017derbent; @gadjiev2013]. Border settlements on the Rubas river are checked against the 1,5k-2k catacomb mounds of the Palasa-Syrt cemetery from the 4th and 5th centuries AD [@gadjiev2008palasa; @gmyrya2012; @saipudi2020palasa].

For the 16th to 18th centuries (1500-1800AD), Russian embassy reports (*Posolskiy Prikaz*), Terki and Kizlyar fortress registers and local Arabic chronicles and law codes (*Tarikh Dagestan*, *Darband-nama*, the *Codex of Rustam Khan* and the 1635 decrees of Maisum Ali-Bek) record household (*dvor* or *dym*) and militia totals across the principalities and free village unions [@aliev1975feudal; @umakhanov1973mutual; @aliev2017tabasaran; @dadaev2014]. Taking 5-5,5 persons per mountain household and 4,5 inhabitants per fighting man gives a total of 460k (420k-500k) in 1700AD and 525k (475k-575k) in 1800AD [@kabuzan1996].

Finally, late 19th-century estimates (1860-1900AD) come from the 1866-1867 military surveys of Dagestan Oblast, the 1886 family lists (*posemeynye spiski*) and the 1897 Russian imperial census, combining the nine districts (*okrugs*) of Dagestan Oblast with the Khasavyurt and Kizlyar lowland districts of Terek Oblast that lie within modern Dagestan [@kabuzan1996; @kozubsky1895; @kozubsky1901; @troynitskiy1905dagestan; @nagieva2005].

## Mesolithic and Neolithic Foundations: Chokh and the Inner Plateaus

Between 10000 and 6000BC, hunter-gatherers lived in two main areas: the limestone rock-shelters of the interior plateaus (1.100-1.800 m) and the old sea terraces along the Caspian coast at Tarki, Manas and Ulluchay. Excavations by V. G. Kotovich (1955-1957) and Hizri Amirkhanov (1980-1985 and 2020-2022) at Chokh in the Gunib district (1.675 m) uncovered six occupation layers (Layers F-A) spanning the transition from foraging to farming in the north-eastern Caucasus [@amirkhanov1987chokh; @amirkhanov2022chokh; @kotovich1964stone; @davudov2009].

The Mesolithic layers (Layers E-C, c. 9000-6500BC) contain small flint tools and bones of East Caucasian tur, wild goat, mouflon and red deer. Seasonal camps in the Chokh and Rugudja gorges (Rugudja, Kozma-Noho and Mekegi) held bands of 25-50 people, giving a total population of 1k-1,8k across Dagestan between 10000 and 8000BC.

Around 6000BC (Layers B-A, c. 6000-5000BC), Chokh provides the earliest evidence for local farming and herding in the North Caucasus [@amirkhanov1987chokh; @davudov2014]. Grain impressions identified by N. R. Yanushevich and G. N. Lisitsyna show that the inhabitants grew six-row naked and hulled barley alongside bread wheat and emmer. Domestic sheep and goats made up more than 60% of the animal bones, and the camp was rebuilt with permanent dry-stone houses, clay floors and stone hearths [@amirkhanov1987chokh; @amirkhanov2022chokh]. Farming raised the regional population from 4,5k (3k-6,5k) in 6000BC to 7,5k (5k-10,5k) by 5000BC, with over 60% living on the interior plateaus (Zone 3).

## Eneolithic and Early Bronze Age: Ginchi, Velikent and the Kura-Araxes Culture

During the 5th millennium BC (5000-3600BC), permanent stone-walled farming villages spread across the mountain basins of interior Dagestan. Excavations by M. G. Gadzhiev at Ginchi (1.650 m in the Gidatl valley) and Chinna uncovered closely packed round stone houses (4-5,5 m across), defensive walls, obsidian blades brought from Transcaucasia and copper awls [@gadzhiev1991early; @gadzhiev1995metallurgy]. Each village held 15-30 families (75-150 people), bringing the regional population to 16k (12k-22k) by 4000BC.

Between 3600 and 2000BC, settlement expanded under the North-Eastern Caucasian branch of the Kura-Araxes culture [@magomedov2000kura; @magomedov2005; @gadzhiev1991early]. On the coastal plain (at Velikent, Kabaz-Kutan, Torpakh-Kala and Dzhemikentskiy), joint Dagestani-American excavations (1994-1998) led by M. G. Gadzhiev, Philip L. Kohl and Rabadan G. Magomedov at Velikent - 25 km north-west of Derbent on the old Ulluchay river fan - showed that five clay mounds (Mounds I-V) covering 280 ha were occupied from c. 3600 to 1900BC [@gadzhiev1997velikent; @gadzhiev2000; @kohl2007making]. Multi-room mudbrick buildings, wheel-made storage jars and over 1,5k bronze weapons, ornaments and casting moulds point to a coastal craft and farming town of 1,2k-2,5k inhabitants [@gadzhiev1995metallurgy; @gadzhiev1997velikent].

Excavations of 13 underground collective catacomb tombs on Mounds III-V at Velikent uncovered 100 to 350 skeletons per tomb; Tomb 1 on Mound III alone held around 300 bodies and more than 1,5k bronze and carnelian grave goods [@gadzhiev1997velikent]. Skeletal studies by M. B. Mednikova and V. Y. Bakholdina show a farming population that practised skull trepanation with high survival rates and buried family members in the same vaults over 150-250 years [@mednikova2020velikent; @bakholdina2008velikent; @davudov2006]. Across all four zones, Kura-Araxes settlement raised Dagestan's population to 45k (35k-55k) by 3000BC and 62k (50k-75k) by 2000BC.

## Middle and Late Bronze and Early Iron Ages: Kayakent-Khorochoi and Highland Terracing

During the Middle Bronze Age (Gemetyube I-II, Velikent and Irganay) and the Late Bronze and Early Iron Age Kayakent-Khorochoi culture (1300-600BC), settlement thickened in both the foothills (Kayakent, Tarki, Karabudakhkent and Zandak) and the interior plateaus (Khorochoi, Gagatli, Kuli and Chirkei) [@kruglov1958ne; @kotovich1982problems; @abakarov1993atlas]. Stone-cist cemeteries of 50 to 400 graves stood beside fortified ridge villages (2-8 ha) built in tiered stone masonry.

Soil dating and field surveys led by A. V. Borisov, D. S. Korobov and I. A. Idrisov between 2012 and 2024 settled the debate begun by M. A. Aglarov [@aglarov1986terraces] over the age of Dagestan's mountain terraces [@borisov2013terraces; @korobov2020terraces; @shaev2024terraces; @idrisov2018; @peters2014]. Radiocarbon dates from buried soils beneath stone terrace walls in the Gunib, Lak and Akusha basins show that hillside terracing began in the Middle to Late Bronze Age (c. 1700-1300BC) and filled the valleys during the Early Iron Age and classical Albanian period [@borisov2013terraces; @korobov2020terraces]. Satellite mapping by Shaev, Borisov, Idrisov and Korobov (2024) shows that man-made terraces cover 48,3% of mid-mountain Dagestan (ranging from 29,4% to 64,8% across individual valleys), far ahead of any other part of the Greater Caucasus (16,1% in the Kislovodsk basin, 9,4% in North Ossetia and 5,9% in Ingushetia; Figure 2) [@shaev2024terraces]. This 100k-150k ha network of terraced fields raised the regional population to 78k (62k-95k) by 1500BC and 95k (75k-115k) by 1000BC.

## Caucasian Albania, Sassanian *Bab al-Abwab* and the Palasa-Syrt Cemetery

Between the 4th century BC and the 4th century AD, the Caspian coastal corridor and foothill valleys formed the northern borderlands of Caucasian Albania and the Sarmatian-Maskut tribes [@kotovich1982problems; @gadjiev2008palasa; @gadjiev2002]. Dozens of mudbrick and cobble-walled towns (*gorodishcha* of 5-25 ha) grew up along the coastal plain at Tarki, Urtseki, Karabudakhkent, Torpakh-Kala and on Derbent hill, lifting the regional population from 115k (90k-140k) in 500BC to 150k (120k-180k) at 1AD and 175k (140k-210k) in 400AD.

In the 5th and 6th centuries AD, the Sassanian shahs Yazdegerd II (438-457), Peroz (459-484) and Khosrow I Anushirvan (531-579) turned the Derbent pass into the great stone fortress of Derbent (*Bab al-Abwab*) [@kudryavtsev1982derbent; @gadjiev2008; @gadjiev2013; @gadjiev2017derbent; @gadjiev2016dagbary]. Replacing Yazdegerd II's mudbrick wall (*Gil-Bary*) of the 440s AD, Khosrow I built around 567-569AD (as recorded in 29 Middle Persian inscriptions studied by M. S. Gadjiev) the twin stone walls 3,6 km long and 350-450 m apart, enclosing 145 ha between the 15 ha *Naryn-Kala* citadel and the sea moles, together with the 42 km *Dag-Bary* mountain wall of 31 stone forts and towers running up into Tabasaran [@kudryavtsev1982derbent; @gadjiev2016dagbary; @gadjiev2017derbent]. Based on Kudryavtsev's study of the 30-35 ha residential town and garrison quarters, Sassanian and early Islamic Derbent held 15k-25k inhabitants (20k in 600AD), rising to 35k-50k at its 10th-century peak under the Hashimid emirs, when al-Istakhri described it as larger than Ardabil [@kudryavtsev1982derbent; @kudryavtsev1993].

Twenty-five kilometres south of Derbent on the Rubas river ridge, the Palasa-Syrt cemetery (4,5 km long, excavated by V. G. Kotovich, L. B. Gmyrya and M. S. Gadjiev) contains 1,5k to 2k earthen mounds over catacomb graves from the late 4th and 5th centuries AD [@gadjiev2008palasa; @gmyrya2012; @saipudi2020palasa; @gmyrya1995huns]. Grave goods and skull shaping point to a mixed Alanic, Maskut and Hunnic border garrison of 3,5k-5k people guarding the Derbent pass over four or five generations [@gadjiev2008palasa; @gmyrya1995huns].

## Early and High Middle Ages: Khazar Cities, *Sarir*, Islamisation and the Mongol and Timurid Invasions

Between 650 and 965AD, northern and coastal Dagestan formed the early urban heartland of the Khazar Khaganate and the Caspian Huns (*Savirs*), while the interior plateaus were united under the Christian and pagan Avar kingdom of Sarir (with its capital at Khunzakh) and the early principalities of Lakz, Tabasaran, Zirikhgeran (Kubachi), Kaitag and Gumik (Kumukh) [@magomedov1983khazar; @gadzhiev1971varachan; @minorsky1958bab; @fedchenko2023]. Excavations in the northern foothills and coastal corridor have uncovered four large walled towns (Figure 3B). Balanjar (Verkhniy Chir-Yurt where the Sulak leaves the foothills) enclosed 110 ha behind a 2,5 km stone and mudbrick wall, with three large cemeteries (over 2k burials) and two early Christian churches; it held 12k-18k people before the Arab general al-Jarrah ibn Abdallah captured it in 722/723AD [@magomedov1983khazar; @fedchenko2023]. Samandar (on the Tarki and Makhachkala plain) covered more than 50 ha of stone terraces and vineyards (al-Mas'udi and Ibn Hawqal reported 40k vineyards before Svyatoslav's attack in 965-969AD) and housed 10k-15k people [@magomedov1983khazar; @abakarov1993atlas]. Varachan (Urtseki), capital of the Caspian Huns, had a 38-40 ha three-tiered stone citadel and farming suburb of 6k-10k inhabitants [@gadzhiev1971varachan; @gmyrya1995huns], while Andreyaulem (Endirey on the Aktash river) was a 65 ha walled town of 8k-12k people guarding the Terek-Sulak crossroads [@magomedov1983khazar; @abakarov1993atlas; @khapizov2019].

During the High Middle Ages (1000-1220AD), the spread of Sunni Islam (at Kala-Koreysh, Kumukh, Richa and Tsakhur, where a madrasa opened in 1075AD) and the growth of mountain craft towns (Kubachi armourers, Sulevkent potters and the market towns of Khunzakh and Kumukh) lifted Dagestan's population to 310k (270k-350k) around 1200AD [@abakarov1993atlas; @minorsky1958bab; @aliev2017tabasaran].

Two waves of invasion broke this medieval growth [@gasanov2024; @dadaev2014]. During the Mongol campaigns of 1220-1222 and 1239-1240, Subutai and Jebe bypassed Derbent in 1221, and Bukdai sacked Derbent, Richa (where a 1239 Arabic inscription records the slaughter), Kumukh (1240) and the coastal plain [@minorsky1958bab; @aliev2017tabasaran]. The lowland towns shrank sharply - William of Rubruck noted Derbent's reduced walls in 1254 - pulling the regional population down to 265k (225k-300k) by 1300AD. After defeating Tokhtamysh on the Terek in April 1395, Timur ravaged the Kumyk plain, Kaitag, Akusha, Nerges and the foothill forts during his 1395-1396 campaigns [@aliev1975feudal; @aliev2017tabasaran; @gasanov2024]. The population fell to a late medieval low of 230k (195k-265k) in 1400AD, with 65% of the survivors living on the interior plateaus and in the Samur gorges (Zone 3).

## Early Modern Principalities and Free *Jamaat* Unions

Between 1450 and 1700AD, Dagestan's population recovered steadily, rising from 285k in 1500AD to 365k in 1600AD and 460k (420k-500k) in 1700AD. Archival studies by B. G. Aliev and M.-S. K. Umakhanov and ethnographic work by M. A. Aglarov [@aliev1975feudal; @umakhanov1973mutual; @aliev2019unions; @aliev2019jamaat; @aglarov1988jamaat; @guseynova2008; @isaev2011] show that 17th-century Dagestan was split between lowland and foothill principalities (about 45% of the population) and self-governing mountain village unions (about 55%) (Figure 3A and Table 2).

Among the principalities, the Shamkhalate of Tarki and the Endirey Kumyk lands were centred on Tarki (1,5k-2k households or 8k-10k people when visited by Adam Olearius in 1638, Evliya Çelebi in 1666 and Jan Struys in 1670), Kafir-Kumukh, Buynak and Endirey (around 1,5k households). Russian *Posolskiy Prikaz* records from 1614-1650 credit the Shamkhal and the Endirey rulers with 12k-15k horsemen and foot soldiers, representing 12k-16k households or 65k-85k people [@umakhanov1973mutual; @aliev1975feudal]. The Kaitag Utsmiate, covering Lower Kaitag (Madzhalis and Bashly, with 1,5k households) and Upper Kaitag/Dargwa (Urkarakh and Kubachi) under the early 17th-century *Codex of Rustam Khan*, fielded 15k-20k warriors from 15k-19k households (80k-100k people) [@aliev1975feudal; @umakhanov1973mutual]. The Kazikumukh Khanate in the Lak basin, centred on Kumukh (1,2k-1,5k stone houses), had 7k-8,5k households (38k-46k people) [@umakhanov1973mutual], while the Avar Nutsalate on the Khunzakh plateau (700-1k households in Khunzakh and the Tobot villages) had 6k-7,5k core households (32k-42k people) [@aliev1975feudal; @aglarov1988jamaat; @saidov1980]. In the south, the Principality of Tabasaran, recorded in the 1635 decrees of Maisum Ali-Bek [@dadaev2014], had 6,5k-8k households (35k-45k people) [@aliev2017tabasaran], and the Safavid governorate of Derbent (after Shah Abbas I retook the city in 1606 and settled Bayat and Qurchi garrisons there) contained Derbent city (2k-2,5k houses, or 10k-14k townspeople) and its coastal villages, totalling 4k-5,5k households or 20k-30k inhabitants [@ikhilov1960narody; @kudryavtsev1982derbent].

In the mountains, over 60 free village unions (*vol'nye obshchestva* or *jamaats*), ruled by elected elders and customary law (*adat*), held the Dargwa plateaus and the Avar, Andi, Dido and Samur gorges [@aliev2019unions; @aliev2019jamaat; @aglarov1988jamaat; @guseynova2008; @isaev2011]. The Akusha-Dargo Upper Dargwa union (Akusha, Tsudakhar, Usisha, Mugi and Mekegi) numbered 9k-11k households (48k-60k people); the Avar, Andi and Dido free unions (Gidatl, Andalal around Chokh and Sogratl, Karata, Bagulal, Chamalyal, Tindi, Dido, Antsukh, Dzhurmut, Koysubulu and Antl-Ratl) totalled 16k-20k households (85k-110k people) [@aglarov1988jamaat; @aliev2019unions; @guseynova2008]; and the Samur valley unions and Elisu Sultanate (Akhty-para, Dokuz-para, Altı-para, Rutul and Tsakhur/Elisu) had 11k-13,5k households (60k-75k people) [@ikhilov1960narody; @aliev2019unions].

## The Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries

In the 18th and 19th centuries, Dagestan suffered two sharp wartime drops before growing rapidly under Russian rule after 1860 [@kabuzan1996; @aliev1999; @aliev2001; @nagieva2005].

In the 1720s, uprisings against Safavid rule in southern Dagestan and Peter I's Persian campaign of 1722-1723 (which built the fortress of Svyatoy Krest on the Sulak and placed Russian garrisons at Derbent and Tarki before Kizlyar was founded on the Terek in 1735) disrupted farming along the coast. Worse damage followed during the three campaigns of the Iranian ruler Nadir Shah in 1734, 1735 and 1741-1743 [@aliev1999; @aliev2001]. Before the combined Avar, Lak and Dargwa militia defeated him at Andalal (Sogratl and Chokh) and Aymaki in September 1741, Nadir Shah burned dozens of villages across Kaitag, Tabasaran, Mehtuli and Kazikumukh, reducing Dagestan's population from 460k in 1700AD to 445k (400k-490k) in 1750AD. Half a century of recovery and growing trade through Kizlyar, Derbent and Tarki then raised the population to 525k (475k-575k) by 1800AD [@kabuzan1996; @aliev1999].

Russia's annexation of the Derbent, Baku and Quba khanates (confirmed by the 1813 Treaty of Gulistan) and General A. P. Yermolov's campaigns of 1818-1826 (building the forts of Vnezapnaya at Endirey in 1819 and Burnaya above Tarki in 1821) sparked the rise of the Caucasian Imamate under the three Imams Ghazi Muhammad (1829-1832), Hamzat Bek (1832-1834) and Shamil (1834-1859) [@kabuzan1996; @magomeddadaev2006]. Thirty years of sieges (at Gimry in 1832, Akhulgo in 1839, Dargo in 1845, Gergebil and Salta in 1847, Chokh in 1849 and Gunib in 1859), cholera outbreaks, crop burning and the emigration of 15k-20k Dagestani *muhajirs* to the Ottoman Empire after 1859 reduced the population to 485k (440k-530k) around 1850AD [@kabuzan1996; @nagieva2005; @magomeddadaev2006].

After Shamil's surrender at Gunib on 25 August 1859, the Russian government created Dagestan Oblast in 1860, with its capital at Temir-Khan-Shura (modern Buynaksk) and nine districts (*okrugs*): Avar, Andi, Gunib, Dargwa, Kazikumukh, Kaitag-Tabasaran, Kyurin, Samur and Temir-Khan-Shura. The northern Kumyk and Nogai plains beyond the Sulak (the Khasavyurt and Kizlyar districts) were placed in Terek Oblast [@kozubsky1895; @adzhiev2018kumyks; @khapizov2015andotsez]. Military counts in the 1860s recorded 450k-480k people in Dagestan Oblast proper, rising in the 1886 family lists to 592,8k [@kozubsky1895; @kabuzan1996; @nagieva2005]. In the First General Census of the Russian Empire on 28 January 1897 [@troynitskiy1905dagestan; @kozubsky1901], Dagestan Oblast had 571,2k present inhabitants - lower than the permanent population because 50k-80k mountain men (*otkhodniki*) were away for the winter working in the Baku oilfields, Tiflis and the Terek towns. By language, the oblast included 158,6k Avars and Ando-Tsez peoples (27,8%), 121,4k Dargwas and Kubachis (21,3%), 94,6k Lezgins (16,6%), 76,4k Laks (13,4%), 32,6k Kumyks in Temir-Khan-Shura and Kaitag (5,7%), 32,1k Azerbaijanis and Tats around Derbent (5,6%) and 22k Tabasarans, Aguls, Rutuls and Tsakhurs [@troynitskiy1905dagestan; @kozubsky1901; @khapizov2015andotsez]. Adding the Khasavyurt district (70,8k inhabitants in 1897, including 26,6k Kumyks and 18,1k Aukh Chechens) and the Dagestani part of the Kizlyar district (Kizlyar town, the Terek Cossack *stanitsas* and the Karanogai steppe camps, with 45k-50k people) gives a total population within modern Dagestan of 690k (650k-730k, or 13,72 persons/km²) by 1900AD [@kabuzan1996; @adzhiev2018kumyks; @nagieva2005]. The opening of the Vladikavkaz Railway through Petrovsk-Port (Makhachkala, 9,8k inhabitants in 1897) to Derbent (14,6k inhabitants) and Baku between 1893 and 1900 started rapid urban growth along the coast, bringing Zone 1 to 124k and Zone 4 to 83k by 1900AD [@nagieva2005].

# Limitations

Three main problems affect population estimates for Dagestan. First, rises and falls in the level of the Caspian Sea between -34 m in the 6th-10th centuries AD and -22 m in the 14th-17th centuries flooded the sea walls of Derbent and several coastal Bronze Age sites while shifting the channels of the lower Terek and Sulak delta [@kudryavtsev1982derbent; @gadzhiev1997velikent]. Second, although terraces cover 48,3% of mid-mountain Dagestan [@shaev2024terraces], fallow rotation and the abandonment of smaller villages after Timur's invasion mean that only 45-65% of the terraced land was farmed at any one time [@borisov2013terraces; @korobov2020terraces]. Third, in the 17th century the Shamkhal of Tarki, the Utsmi of Kaitag and the Khan of Kazikumukh often claimed the same border village unions when dealing with Russian envoys, so raw militia totals have to be reduced by 10-15% to avoid double counting [@aliev1975feudal; @umakhanov1973mutual]. Conversely, in the January 1897 census the winter absence of 50k-80k migrant workers in Baku and Terek Oblast lowered the count in the mountain districts compared with the 1886 family lists [@kozubsky1901; @nagieva2005].

# Conclusion

Between 10000BC and 1900AD, Dagestan grew from an early mountain farming centre at Chokh (4,5k in 6000BC) into the most heavily terraced and urbanised part of the eastern Caucasus, with 690k people (13,72 persons/km²) by 1900AD. The pairing of walled trading towns along the Caspian coast (Velikent, Derbent, Urtseki, Tarki, Balanjar and Petrovsk-Port) with terraced stone villages on the interior plateaus (Chokh, Khunzakh, Kumukh, Akusha and Kubachi) allowed Dagestan to weather the Mongol and Timurid invasions, Nadir Shah's campaigns and the Caucasian War with much smaller long-term population losses than the open plains of central and north-western Ciscaucasia.
